relinquish

/rih-LING-kwish/ · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Relinquish means to give up or let go of a possession, position, right, or control — often formally, and often reluctantly.

After her third ankle injury, Marisol agreed to relinquish the team captaincy so a healthier teammate could lead the squad.

Example

At eighty-nine, Mr. Alvarez finally agreed to relinquish his driver's license after his doctor explained how much his eyesight had declined.

Mr. Alvarez gives up a privilege he has held for decades, formally and reluctantly — exactly the kind of letting-go that relinquish describes.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

surrender: Surrender means to give something up under pressure — an opponent or circumstance has forced the choice, as when an army surrenders a city. Relinquish is quieter: you let go of a post, right, or grip, often reluctantly but not necessarily defeated. A cornered army surrenders; a retiring chair relinquishes the gavel.

cede: Cede means to formally yield something to another party, especially territory or power, usually by treaty or agreement — an empire cedes islands. Relinquish needs no recipient and no negotiation: you can relinquish a claim, a license, or your grip on a rope with nobody taking it over.

waive: Waive means to voluntarily decline to enforce a right, fee, or requirement — a bank waives a fee. What is waived is set aside before it is ever used. Relinquish means letting go of something already in your hands: control, a seat, a grip. You waive a claim before exercising it; you relinquish what you hold.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

retain: to keep possession of

withhold: to refuse to hand over

Where it sits · how permanently you let go — yield → relinquish → forfeit

yield vs. relinquish: Yield is milder than relinquish: a driver who yields at an intersection gives way for a moment and then moves on.

forfeit vs. relinquish: Forfeit is stronger than relinquish: a team that forfeits a match loses it outright as a penalty, with no say in the matter.

The pieces

Prefix — re-

Prefix — re-: back, behind

Root — linqu

Root — linqu: to leave (Latin linquere)

Suffix — -ish

Suffix — -ish: verb-forming ending (from Old French -iss-)

Put it together

Put it together: From Latin relinquere: re- (behind) + linquere (to leave) — to leave something behind, letting it go for good.

Word Choice

Formal / neutral

Relinquish is about letting go of something you actually hold — control, a claim, a seat, even a physical grip ("he relinquished his hold on the rope"). It often suggests reluctance or formality. Its unit-mate renunciation is a more deliberate, often public rejection of a belief or claim: you relinquish the wheel, but you announce a renunciation of a throne.
